title: China's churches
hook: registered and house churches, growing through persecution

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korean prayer mountains, and a room praying aloud before sunrise. Your line was dawn prayer. Did the first minute of your morning go anywhere new? Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

Two Sunday mornings in the same Chinese city. In the first, a church with its name on the gate. The doors are open, the choir is robed, the hymn numbers are on a board at the front, and the church is registered with the state. In the second, an apartment a few streets away. Curtains drawn. Folding chairs borrowed from the neighbors who don't ask questions. Someone is keeping the singing soft. Both rooms are reading the same Gospel. Both are being watched, in different ways. Today, China's churches, and a seed you can't see.
screen: `A CHURCH WITH ITS NAME ON THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Christians in China gather in roughly two ways. Registered churches belong to bodies the government recognizes, and meet openly under state rules about what can be taught and who can attend. House churches meet outside that system, in homes, offices, rented rooms. The line between them is not always neat, and Christians in China disagree about it honestly. Some register so they can worship in the open and serve within the law. Others refuse because they will not let the state decide what happens in worship. Reports from China describe hard seasons for both: crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained. And still the people keep meeting. Nobody can count them exactly, because a church in a living room keeps no public list. Jesus talked about growth you can't watch. In John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." A corn of wheat is just a grain. It has to go under before anything comes up. And in Mark, a man scatters seed and goes to bed, and the seed grows while he sleeps and wakes: "the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." He knoweth not how. The farmer isn't in charge of it. The soil is dark, and the growing happens there. There's an old saying, traced back to an early Christian writer named Tertullian, that the blood of Christians is seed. Christians in China would not all put it that way, and the old line is no reason to romanticize suffering. Some readers hear the same picture in what Jesus said: under the ground is not the same as gone.
screen: `A CORN OF WHEAT FALLS INTO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the people meeting today with the curtains drawn. Settle, and breathe. Picture the two rooms from the start, the church with its name on the gate and the apartment a few streets away. Picture someone in each one, an older woman with a worn Bible, a young man keeping one eye on the door. You don't know their names. Hold them anyway. If you pray, you can pray for Christians in China, in both kinds of room, in whatever words you have. If you don't, simply wish them safety and courage, and let the picture stay for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
China's churches. Registered churches meeting in the open, and house churches meeting outside registration: two ways of gathering, under pressure, around the same Gospel.
Your line: the seed underground. Today, when something good you've planted seems to be doing nothing, remember the farmer asleep while it grows, he knoweth not how. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians elsewhere pray for the church in China in their own prayers and in services; in China, registered congregations meet in church buildings, while house churches gather in homes and other private spaces.

notes: Claims rule: no numbers, growth figures or dates given; the index hook's 'growing' is rendered as 'still the people keep meeting' and 'nobody can count them exactly'. Confirm this is fair to the outline.

Registered churches are not named (Three-Self Patriotic Movement / China Christian Council for Protestants; the Catholic Patriotic Association and the unregistered Catholic communities are not discussed). A Keeper may want a sentence on Catholics in China.

'Reports from China describe ... crosses taken down from church roofs, gatherings closed, pastors detained': widely reported (e.g. Zhejiang cross removals, Early Rain Covenant Church), but no specifics or dates given; confirm wording is fair and not inflammatory.
The two stances on registration are described without ranking; confirm fairness to both.

Tertullian, Apology 50: the Latin is usually rendered 'the blood of Christians is seed'; the popular 'blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church' is a later paraphrase. Paraphrased with quoted: null; confirm.
The hook scene (a registered church and an apartment house church in one city) is illustrative, not a specific report.
